title: What is the McKinsey interview process, and how should you prepare?
description: McKinsey's hiring steps explained: application, the Solve assessment, Personal Experience Interviews and interviewer-led cases, with preparation tips.
hook: The McKinsey process usually runs from an online application to Solve, a game-based online assessment used for many roles, then two rounds of interviews in which each interview pairs a Personal Experience Interview with a case, and finally an offer. The cases are usually interviewer-led, so you answer a sequence of focused questions rather than steering yourself. The process is intense but well documented, which means you can prepare for every part of it.
body:
In this guide

  • The steps
  • Solve
  • The Personal Experience Interview
  • The case: interviewer-led
  • A worked example of an interviewer-led case
  • How to prepare
  • Common mistakes
  • Practical rules: AI, video and scams
  • Practice
  • Where to go next

The steps

Details vary by office, role and year, and your recruiter confirms them in advance. A typical path for a client-facing generalist role:

  1. Online application. Your CV, and in some offices a cover letter and transcripts.
  2. Solve. An online, game-based assessment for many roles.
  3. First-round interviews. Commonly two or three interviews of 45 to 60 minutes, each combining a Personal Experience Interview (PEI) and a case.
  4. Final-round interviews. A similar format with more senior interviewers, usually partners, and often more open-ended cases.
  5. Offer.

McKinsey's interviewing page says that for most client-facing roles you will have PEI and problem-solving interviews, with expertise interviews for some roles, and that the number of interviews depends on the role.

Solve

McKinsey describes Solve as a gamified assessment that tests your natural problem-solving abilities, and says there is no need to prepare: approach it with curiosity and creativity. The scenarios are ecological or scientific rather than business ones, and the modules change over time.

What does help is general comfort with reading data, making decisions under time pressure and checking your work, which your case preparation builds anyway. Follow the instructions in your invitation and make sure your setup is stable. Online tests and digital cases has the wider picture of firm assessments.

The Personal Experience Interview

Each interview includes a deep conversation about one real moment from your life. McKinsey's page asks you to prepare two personal examples for each of four areas, to choose experiences that genuinely mattered to you, to lead with your reasoning rather than just your actions, and to be ready for a conversation, not a rehearsed story. Guides that track the page in 2026 describe the four areas as leadership, connection (building relationships and persuading people), drive (achieving something difficult through your own initiative) and growth (learning and changing, including from failure).

The interviewer will probe: what exactly did you do, why that and not something else, what did the other person say, what would you change? A story that survives five follow-up questions beats a polished two-minute monologue.

Compare two openings to a leadership story.

"Our team was behind on a project, so I organised everyone and we finished on time."
"Two weeks before our deadline, one of four teammates stopped turning up. I had to decide whether to cover his work quietly or confront it. I chose to speak to him first, because I suspected something was wrong outside the course, and that conversation changed how we split the work."

The second gives a specific moment, a real decision and the reasoning behind it, which is what the follow-ups will dig into. How to build your stories and the leadership question go further.

The case: interviewer-led

McKinsey cases are usually interviewer-led. The interviewer presents the problem, then asks a series of questions: your structure, then perhaps a chart, a calculation, a brainstorm and a final recommendation. They choose what you analyse next. Your job is to answer each question well, state what it means, and be ready to move on.

McKinsey's page stresses that there is not one logical solution and that it wants tailored thinking rather than standard frameworks. So build a structure for the specific problem in front of you. How to structure a case shows how.

A worked example of an interviewer-led case

Prompt: A sportswear brand sells only through retailers. It is considering launching its own online store. Should it? (Illustrative numbers.)

Question 1: "What would you want to know?"

A tailored structure: (1) the economics, meaning how much more the brand earns per item sold online, minus the cost of running the store; (2) demand, meaning how many customers would buy direct; (3) retailer reaction, since retailers might cut orders; (4) capabilities: logistics, returns, marketing.

Question 2: "Here is the data. What is the profit impact?"

The store is expected to take 400,000 orders a year at an average of $80. The brand keeps 35% of the price online but earns 20% when the same item sells through a retailer. Running the store costs $4M a year.

  • Online margin per order: $80 × 35% = $28. Wholesale margin: $80 × 20% = $16.
  • Extra margin per order: $28 − $16 = $12, assuming these customers would otherwise have bought through a retailer.
  • Extra margin in total: 400,000 × $12 = $4.8M.
  • Net of running costs: $4.8M − $4M = $0.8M a year.
  • Break-even: $4M ÷ $12 ≈ 333,000 orders.

The trap is to say the store earns 400,000 × $28 = $11.2M. Most of that profit would have been earned anyway through retailers. Only the extra $12 per order is new.

Question 3: "What risks do you see?"

Group them: retailers reducing orders or shelf space; orders falling short of 333,000; higher returns and delivery costs than planned; and a need for capabilities the brand does not have.

Question 4: "What do you recommend?"

"Launch, but carefully. The store adds about $0.8M a year, with break-even at about 333,000 orders, so the cushion is only about 17%. The biggest risk is retailer reaction, so I'd launch a limited range first and agree terms with our largest retailers before scaling."

Each answer is short, quantified and ends with a "so what". That is what an interviewer-led case rewards.

How to prepare

  • Work through McKinsey's official practice cases on its interviewing page: Beautify, Diconsa, Electro-Light, Transforming a national education system and Talbot Trucks, as listed in 2026. They contain suggested answers.
  • Practise interviewer-led cases with a partner who asks specific questions in order. Many cases in our casebook work well this way.
  • Prepare at least two PEI stories for each of the four areas, rehearse them out loud and have a friend probe with "why?" and "what exactly did you do?"
  • Practise mental maths and chart reading daily in the maths drills.

Common mistakes

  • Treating the PEI as a warm-up. It is assessed seriously in every interview. Under-prepared stories fall apart under follow-up questions.
  • Reciting a framework. Interviewers want a structure built for this problem.
  • Answering the question you expected. If the interviewer asks only for causes, give causes, not your whole plan.
  • Stopping at the number. "$0.8M" is half an answer. "$0.8M, with a thin cushion, so launch carefully" is a whole one.

Practical rules: AI, video and scams

McKinsey's interviewing page encourages using AI to explain concepts while you prepare, but does not allow generating answers in real time during an interview, and asks you to disable AI tools such as note-takers or assistants. For virtual interviews it asks you to find a quiet, private space and keep your camera on.

McKinsey also warns that its recruiting never involves interviewing by instant message, never requires you to buy products or services, and that genuine staff use addresses ending in @mckinsey.com or @external.mckinsey.com.

Practice

1. In the online store case, retailers respond by cutting orders, costing the brand $1.5M of wholesale margin a year. Should it still launch?

Show the answer

Net impact becomes $0.8M − $1.5M = −$0.7M a year, so not on these terms. To break even, the store would need another $0.7M ÷ $12 ≈ 58,000 orders, about 458,000 in total, or the brand would need to protect retailer relationships, for example with an online-only range.

2. Give a one-sentence answer to "Why that approach?" for the leadership story above.

Show the answer

"Covering his work would have fixed the deadline but not the problem, and I thought something was wrong, so I wanted to understand it before deciding anything." It explains the reasoning and the alternative you rejected, which is exactly what the follow-up is probing.

Where to go next

Compare with the BCG process, read how to move a case forward for the moments when even a McKinsey interviewer asks what you would do next, and confirm every detail of your own process with your recruiter.
